ballard-locks.name: Ballard Locks (Hiram M. Chittenden Locks) & fish ladder
ballard-locks.blurb: Boats from kayaks to fishing trawlers rise and fall 26 ft between Puget Sound and the lakes; salmon climb a 21-weir fish ladder past underwater windows; a botanical garden on the north bank.

spawn.note: North bank by the Administration Building looking south over the large lock.

extent.description: Carl S. English Jr. Botanical Garden and visitor centre (north), walkways across the lock walls and gates, large and small locks, spillway dam with tainter gates, south bank fish ladder + underground viewing room, Commodore Park edge.
extent.edges: Fences at lock edges and the spillway; NW 54th St (north).
extent.vertical: Upstream lake level 20–22 ft above sea level; Puget Sound tidal; lift up to 26 ft (7.9 m).

structures.name: Large lock (1917)
structures.form: Concrete chamber with steel mitre gates, mid-gate, bollards, ladders; lockwall attendants in hard hats; boats tie off; chamber fills/drains in 10–15 min.

structures.name: Small lock
structures.form: Narrow chamber used when traffic is light; pedestrians cross on the gate walkway.

structures.name: Spillway dam
structures.form: Concrete dam with steel tainter gates and smolt flumes; white water when gates open.

structures.name: Fish ladder (rebuilt 1976) + viewing room
structures.form: Stepped concrete channel of 21 weirs on the south bank; below ground a dim viewing gallery with large windows into the ladder where salmon swim past; "Salmon Waves" stainless sculptures (Paul Sorey) at the entrance.

plaques.title: Busiest lock in the US
plaques.text: The Ballard Locks carry more boat traffic than any other lock in the United States.

plaques.title: Lakes lowered
plaques.text: Opening the canal in 1916 lowered Lake Washington by 8.8 ft, drying more than 1,000 acres of wetland.

plaques.title: Two locks
plaques.text: The small lock is 30 × 150 ft and the large lock 80 × 825 ft; boats rise or fall up to 26 ft in 10–15 minutes.

plaques.title: Fish ladder
plaques.text: Rebuilt in 1976 with 21 weirs, the ladder is unusual for sitting where salt and fresh water meet; peak sockeye viewing is July to mid-August.

interaction.primary: Operate a lockage (with an attendant NPC): close the lower gates, open the fill valve, watch the water rise and boats float up, open upper gates.
secondary: Count salmon in the viewing room (seasonal: July–Sept)

iconic.frame: Large lock full of boats from the north wall with the gates and control tower

seasonal: Salmon: sockeye July–mid-Aug, Chinook/coho late summer–autumn
Large lock drained ~2 weeks in November, small lock in March (maintenance)

lines.text: Welcome to the Locks! Stay behind the yellow line, please.

More boat traffic goes through here than any other lock in the United States.
When the canal opened, Lake Washington dropped almost nine feet.
The fish ladder has 21 weirs — salmon jump each one on the way to the lakes.
Sockeye peak is July into August. Bring the kids to the viewing room.
Picnic on the garden lawn, best free show in Ballard.
Boats don't care about rain.
There's a fishing boat coming in from Alaska!

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
